This collection stands on other people’s data, photographs, software, and ideas about teaching. This page credits them.

The course

The problems are built around the traditional UCSC Math 23B section worksheets, Weeks 2 to 10. Every core skill on those worksheets is practiced in a core problem here. The collection, its problems, and this site were designed by Abhinav Jha, who chose the topics, the titles, and the weekly subtitles.

How the problems are written

The way these problems are written (story first, a model that separates published data from assumptions, a whiteboard checklist that begins with a sketch and a prediction, and a final check against reality) draws on the following work. We read each one while revising this collection. Any shortcomings here are our own.

  • UCLA Life Sciences 30 (LS 30A/30B), mathematics for life scientists · Alan Garfinkel and colleagues; see “Teaching Dynamics to Biology Undergraduates: the UCLA Experience,” Bulletin of Mathematical Biology (2022)
    Building a model from plain questions (what makes this quantity go up or down?), giving each term a name students can say aloud, and treating the application as the motivation rather than decoration.
  • GAIMME: Guidelines for Assessment and Instruction in Mathematical Modeling Education · SIAM and COMAP
    Explicit attention to getting from the real problem to the mathematics, and an explicit reconciliation with reality at the end; the self-checks on sign, size, and sensitivity.
  • Calculus in Context · The Five College Calculus Project (Callahan, Hoffman, Cox, O’Shea, Pollatsek, Senechal)
    Stating each assumption with its reason, and saying openly when a simplification fails.
  • The Three Acts of a Mathematical Story · Dan Meyer
    Opening with a vivid question in few words, and asking for a prediction before computing.
  • HiMCM 2023 Problem A · COMAP High School Mathematical Contest in Modeling
    Short, sourced scenarios followed by numbered, verb-led tasks, with loaded terms defined.
  • SIMIODE modeling scenarios (e.g. 1-012, Sublimation) · SIMIODE, Systemic Initiative for Modeling Investigations and Opportunities with Differential Equations
    Reducing a scenario to a few plain questions, and reporting honestly where real data misbehave.
  • Active Calculus Multivariable · Steven Schlicker, David Austin, and Matthew Boelkins
    Motivating questions, asking what one small piece means before the whole, and insisting on units.
  • MIT 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, supplementary notes on two-dimensional flux · Arthur Mattuck, MIT OpenCourseWare
    Naming the physical quantity before the integral, and stating sign conventions in words.
  • Curl and Div (Math 21a handout) · Oliver Knill, Harvard University
    Tying each vector-calculus object to an instrument you could hold: a paddle wheel for curl, a planimeter for Green’s theorem.
  • Practical Meteorology, Chapter 13 exercises · Roland Stull, University of British Columbia (via LibreTexts)
    Exercises that move from apply, to justify, to “what if…”.
  • AOS 610 problem sets · Department of Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences, University of Wisconsin–Madison
    One-sentence physical setups for circulation problems, with conversion facts given inline.
  • MOSAIC Calculus · Daniel Kaplan
    Using dimensions and units as a guide to thinking, and checking whether an answer is “good enough”.

Titles

The collection’s name tips its hat to Jules Verne’s Around the World in Eighty Days (1872). Several weekly subtitles borrow from Charles Dickens (A Tale of Two Cities), Forrest Gump (“life is like a box of chocolates”), Robert Frost (“The Road Not Taken”), Jane Austen (Pride and Prejudice), Star Wars (“May the Force be with you”), and Joe Raposo’s song “Bein’ Green”, sung by Kermit the Frog.

How this was made

Research, drafting, coding, and checking were done with the help of Claude, an AI model by Anthropic, working in Claude Code under the designer’s direction. Every checked answer is re-derived independently in SymPy, every source was opened and read, and every photograph’s license was checked.

Practice with a place in mind.
